title: Class-Balanced Loss Based on Effective Number of Samples
authors: Yin Cui, Menglin Jia, Tsung-Yi Lin, Yang Song, Serge Belongie
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
conclusions: Proposes a theoretical framework treating each sample as covering a small neighboring region in feature space, and derives the 'effective number of samples' E_n = (1-beta^n)/(1-beta) to quantify diminishing marginal information as class sample count n grows.

Introduces the Class-Balanced (CB) loss: a re-weighting term inversely proportional to the effective number of samples per class (1-beta)/(1-beta^{n_y}), applied on top of any base loss (softmax CE, sigmoid CE, or focal loss).
The scheme is model- and loss-agnostic; it only requires knowing the number of training samples per class and a single hyperparameter beta in [0,1).

Shows significant error-rate reductions on long-tailed CIFAR-10/100 (varying imbalance factors 10-200) versus unweighted softmax/sigmoid/focal loss, and improvements on large-scale real long-tailed datasets (iNaturalist 2017/2018) and ILSVRC 2012 with ResNet backbones.

The method re-weights the LOSS per training class based on training-set frequency; it does not constrain or control how many test-time predictions land in any class -- there is no count/quota mechanism at all.
our_use: main.tex:207-214, Related Work paragraph 'Cost-sensitive and imbalanced training': cited alongside elkan2001foundations, lin2017focal, cao2019learning, menon2021logit as an example of loss reweighting/reshaping approaches, with the point that 'None of it guarantees the prediction count; the realized number of constrained-class predictions remains a free outcome. TraLO targets the count directly.' This is an accurate characterization: cui2019class's class-balanced weighting only reweights training loss by inverse effective sample count and provides no test-time count/quota guarantee.
